steps.say: An infant with colicky screaming that comes in waves should raise one diagnosis above all. Intussusception tops the list of bowel blockages between three months and three years, peaking around five to nine months. The telescoping gut drags its own blood supply inward, so hours matter. The anatomical drawing here shows the ileocolic segment swallowing its mesentery, the exact mechanism behind the pain waves.
steps.tx: Treat **peak incidence age** as the diagnostic anchor. Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in infants between 3 months and 3 years, with peak incidence between 5 and 9 months. Ileocolic telescoping (one segment swallowing the next) drags mesentery into the sheath, choking blood supply and turning a mechanical blockage into an ischaemic emergency within hours. Suspect it first in any infant in this window with episodic inconsolable crying, and examine the abdomen between pain waves.

vis.alt: Anatomical illustration of ileocolic telescoping with compressed mesentery beside an ultrasound inset showing the target sign.
vis.caption: Ileocolic telescoping drags mesentery into the sheath, choking blood supply. Peak age is 3 months to 3 years. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Most infant cases have no lump or polyp to blame, just overexcited gut immunity. More than nine in ten under-twos are idiopathic, triggered by viral infections that swell the Peyer's patches into a natural lead point. Adenovirus season brings clusters to every casualty. So a preceding cold or stomach bug in the history supports, rather than distracts from, the diagnosis.
steps.tx: Explain **idiopathic hypertrophy of Peyer patches** as the usual trigger. Over 90% of cases in infants under 2 years are idiopathic ileocolic intussusception triggered by viral gastroenteritis or adenovirus-induced lymphoid hyperplasia (swollen gut immune tissue catching the peristaltic wave). These hyperplastic patches act as a soft lead point that peristalsis then drags forward. No tumour hunt is needed in this age group after successful reduction, though recurrence still warrants standard follow up.

steps.say: The rules flip once the child grows past toddlerhood. Beyond two to three years, a real lead point usually lurks, and Meckel's diverticulum heads the list, followed by duplications, polyps and Burkitt lymphoma of the ileocaecal region. The diagram of lead points shows each culprit exactly where the scan should hunt. So an older child with intussusception earns a full search for the underlying lesion, not just a reduction.
steps.tx: Hunt **pathological lead points** in older children. Children older than 2-3 years frequently have a pathological lead point: Meckel diverticulum (most common, the remnant vitelline pouch), intestinal duplication cyst, polyp, or Burkitt lymphoma. Examine for anaemia, weight loss or a palpable mass suggesting these lesions, and image the abdomen comprehensively even after successful reduction. Burkitt disease demands oncology referral at once, since reduction alone never treats the underlying tumour.

vis.alt: Diagram showing intussusception with various pathological lead points: Meckel's diverticulum, intestinal polyp, and hypertrophied lymphoid tissue.
vis.caption: Pathological lead points for intussusception

steps.say: Forget the textbook picture of pain plus vomiting plus bloody stools all together. That complete triad shows up in under a third of children at first contact, so waiting for it guarantees delay. Far more often you meet episodic screaming with drawn up legs, isolated vomiting, or lethargy between waves. Red currant jelly stool arrives late and signals ischaemia, not early disease.
steps.tx: Remember **classic clinical triad rarity** when assessing. The classic triad of episodic crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, and red currant jelly stools (blood mixed with mucus) is present in under 30-40% of cases at initial presentation. Early features are paroxysmal crying with pallor, vomiting and a sausage shaped abdominal mass, while blood per rectum and lethargy mark later ischaemia (blood starved bowel). Act on partial patterns plus the right age window rather than demanding all three features.

points: Seen in under a third at arrival
right.title: Full textbook triad

steps.say: Ultrasound settles the question at the bedside within minutes when done well. Look for the doughnut or target in cross section, three to five centimetres of layered bowel wall, and the kidney shaped pseudokidney along its length. Sensitivity approaches one hundred percent in practised hands. The inset beside the anatomy drawing captures that unmistakable target, the sign that triggers enema reduction.
steps.tx: Trust **ultrasound diagnostic signs** as the investigation of choice. Abdominal ultrasonography has near 100% sensitivity, showing the pathognomonic target or doughnut sign (3-5 cm diameter layered rings) in transverse view and pseudokidney sign in longitudinal view. Add Doppler assessment of wall blood flow, because absent flow predicts failed reduction and threatened gangrene. A confident positive scan with a stable child proceeds straight to enema reduction without contrast CT delays.

vis.alt: Anatomical illustration of ileocolic telescoping with compressed mesentery beside an ultrasound inset showing the target sign.
vis.caption: Target sign on transverse ultrasound with pseudokidney views lengthwise triggers enema reduction. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Air beats barium for reduction in children: quicker, cleaner and less radiation. Under fluoroscopy or ultrasound guidance, controlled air pressure pushes the telescoped bowel back out, succeeding in eighty five to ninety percent, capped at one hundred twenty millimetres of mercury in infants. Three attempts are reasonable if the child stays stable and each try advances further. Watch the pressure gauge relentlessly, since the colon of an infant tolerates no heroics.
steps.tx: Choose **pneumatic vs hydrostatic reduction** correctly. Air enema (pneumatic reduction) has an 85-90% success rate with lower radiation dose than hydrostatic barium reduction, controlled at maximum pressure of 120 mmHg in infants. Confirm complete reduction by free reflux of air into terminal ileum with disappearance of the soft tissue mass, then observe for recurrence. Failed but stable cases may attempt one careful repeat, while any deterioration aborts further tries immediately.

steps.say: Never push air into a belly with peritonitis, free air or shock. A rigid tender abdomen with guarding means the bowel wall has already failed, and pressurising it blows faeces into the peritoneum. Pneumoperitoneum on plain film or a cold shut down shocked child sends the case straight to theatre. These three findings are absolute, with no room for one cautious attempt first.
steps.tx: Respect the **absolute contraindications to enema** reduction without exception. Evidence of peritonitis (rigid guarding abdomen), pneumoperitoneum (intestinal perforation with free air), or hemodynamic shock constitutes an absolute contraindication to non-operative reduction. Such children go directly for fluid resuscitation, broad spectrum antibiotics and surgical exploration, where manual reduction or resection follows intraoperative findings. Document the contraindication clearly so no subsequent team attempts reduction by mistake.

steps.say: Warn every family before discharge that the bowel can telescope again. About one child in ten recurs after successful air reduction, and more than half of those recurrences strike within the first two to three days. So keep the first observation honest, explain exactly which scream should bring them racing back, and image promptly on return. Most recurrences reduce again by enema; repeated episodes earn a lead point hunt.
steps.tx: Quote the **recurrence rate after reduction** at discharge. Intussusception recurs in approximately 10% of cases following successful air enema reduction, with over half of recurrences occurring within the first 48-72 hours. Admit or closely observe the early window where vigilance is cheapest, and give parents precise return precautions about episodic pain, vomiting or blood. Recurrent cases reduce successfully again in most instances, but three or more episodes mandate elective evaluation for a hidden lead point.
